**Subject: Re: Gelat-oat Production Decision**

Hi, thanks for meeting today.

I'm going to be blunt: I carved out time on my calendar expecting a recommendation, and I didn't get one. You had Carlos's analysis, you had the data, and you had a room with two people ready to listen. What I needed was a clear point of view — which option you're backing, why, what numbers you're watching, and what keeps you up at night about the choice.

I can't greenlight something that wasn't pitched. 

Take the weekend. Come back Monday with an actual recommendation. Show me you've wrestled with the numbers, that you know what good and bad look like in the early weeks, and that you've thought past the spreadsheet to what could break. I need conviction backed by rigor, not silence.

We'll reconvene Monday at 2pm.

Zena

P.S. — I'll send you a six-month update on how this all played out.

narrativeImpact.story: Zena listened, then pressed for the numbers behind our production recommendation. With Carlos in the room, we couldn’t point to clear leading indicators—no active account rate, velocity, or quality signals, and we never stress-tested the 60% adoption assumption. The plan felt more hopeful than engineered. Zena declined to greenlight and sent us back to validate demand, define an early-warning dashboard, and align the team on measurable triggers before Gelat-oat could leave the whiteboard.
narrativeImpact.title: Back to the Drawing Board
narrativeImpact.description: The pitch didn't convince. Launch delayed. Team misaligned.

narrativeImpact.story: Six months after the pitch, Gelat-oat finally came online behind schedule, and the $1.2M fixed-cost clock started ticking before momentum did. We committed to the new plant on a slim base-case lift, but managed the launch through quarterly revenue and profit—rear‑view metrics Zena warned were too slow. As weekly active accounts quietly slipped, no one caught the early erosion until revenue landed 20% under plan, forcing a late scramble in marketing and operations.
narrativeImpact.title: Finding Our Footing
narrativeImpact.description: Delayed timeline. The team was watching lagging indicators instead of leading signals.

narrativeImpact.story: Six months after the pitch, Gelat-oat is beating the high-case curve—because the team treated demand as a hypothesis, not a hope. Derek and Carlos backed the new plant on fixed-cost leverage, then built an early-warning dashboard tracking adoption pace, active rates, repeat orders, and velocity. When adoption softened in week six, they held operations to one shift, protected margins, and reignited the funnel—then ramped confidently as signals turned green.
narrativeImpact.title: Market Maker
narrativeImpact.description: Gelat-oat is thriving. The right production path, strong execution, aligned team.

narrativeImpact.story: Six months after Zena approved the new plant, Gelat-oat is beating the base case and running with consistent quality. Sophie anchored the risk at a 414K breakeven, then set daily leading indicators—adoption, reorder rate, and volume per customer—to steer decisions in real time. Early segmentation reads guided targeted promotions, smoothing velocity and protecting margin. Carlos, energized by the clarity, kept operations tight and capacity flexible as demand surged beyond plan.
narrativeImpact.title: Market Maker
narrativeImpact.description: Gelat-oat is thriving. The right production path, strong execution, aligned team.

narrativeImpact.story: Six months after the pitch, Gelat-oat is on menus—and momentum is real—but the rollout came with scars. The team committed to the new plant and managed cash tightly, tracking weekly active rate and velocity across the 24 pilot restaurants. Yet they didn’t challenge the 60% adoption assumption early enough; when adoption landed closer to 48%, it took weeks to surface. Carlos regrouped, sharpened the account-by-account plan, and demand is climbing again.
narrativeImpact.title: Gaining Traction
narrativeImpact.description: Promising launch with growing pains. Demand is building but not without challenges.

narrativeImpact.story: Six months after Zena’s pitch, Gelat-oat is a standing menu item across the region—and the new plant is humming. We didn’t treat 60% adoption as destiny; we built an early-warning dashboard tracking weekly active accounts, velocity, reorders, and adoption. When adoption landed at 52%, the week‑6 truth moment triggered targeted chef outreach and account sequencing, protecting throughput. Carlos stayed energized, and the plant-scale bet became a controlled win.
narrativeImpact.title: Market Maker
narrativeImpact.description: Gelat-oat is thriving. The right production path, strong execution, aligned team.

narrativeImpact.story: Six months after the retrofit go‑live, Gelat-oat is on shelves and in more kitchens—but the ride hasn’t been smooth. We bet on 60% adoption with a 55% break-even cushion and tracked active accounts and weekly velocity, yet we didn’t challenge the adoption assumption early enough. Actual adoption settled near 48%, and it took weeks to register the gap. Now we’re tightening targeting, reinforcing sales discipline, and rebuilding the forecast with clearer triggers.
narrativeImpact.title: Gaining Traction
narrativeImpact.description: Promising launch with growing pains. Demand is building but not without challenges.

narrativeImpact.story: Six months after the pitch, Gelat-oat is on more menus than planned and holding strong. You backed the new plant for upside, but governed the launch with disciplined triggers: weekly active account rate and a hard “<1% texture complaints” standard. When quality monitoring surfaced an early co-packer texture drift, the team quarantined batches, corrected specs, and protected reorder momentum. With active accounts sustaining 75%, Carlos ramped supply confidently—and the market rewarded it.
narrativeImpact.title: Market Maker
narrativeImpact.description: Gelat-oat is thriving. The right production path, strong execution, aligned team.

events.content: Chapter 1: The Gelat-oat Opportunity has started.

What is this chapter about?
Teams learn more about the new product they are rolling out for Butterfeast, as well as the different production paths they might use to make the product. They use two financial tools, a Scenario Planner and a Breakeven Calculator, to develop an initial hypothesis as to which production path they might want to support.

What to look for:
  • Do teams explore all of the resources?
  • Do they use each of the financial tools?
  • Do they calculate each of the breakeven points correctly?
Remember to move around to listen to teams' discussions. Sometimes the most insightful comments are said from one participant to another, rather than to an AI character.

Suggestion: You might consider using the Send Message feature to remind participants:

Make sure to calculate the Breakeven for each of the three Production Paths.
Reminder: Move teams to the Decision now.
Decision phase has started.

Decision Time! Teams must enter their initial reflections on the three production paths. The question asks: "Are there any options that you would take off the table? Share your reasoning in a sentence." Their answers should provide some insight into their level of understanding of what they just reviewed.

Message sent to participants:
Moving to decision

Chapter 1 ended — showing feedback.

closing breakouts now
Chapter 2: Gauging Demand has started.

What is this chapter about?
Teams now try to get a better understanding of the true demand for Gelat-oat. They have been given an initial Market Opportunity Brief by their colleague Carlos. They then interview Carlos to learn more.

What to look for:
  • Do teams explore all of the resources quickly?
  • Do they explore the different scenarios in the Demand Signal Explorer?
  • Do they ask Carlos questions to get a better understanding of how solid his initial projections are?
Remember to move around to listen to teams' discussions. Sometimes the most insightful comments are said from one participant to another, rather than to an AI character.

Suggestion: You might consider using the Send Message feature to remind participants:

Keep chatting with Carlos. Probe into any assumptions being made in his initial assessment.
Reminder: Move teams to the Decision now.
Decision phase has started.
Decision Time! Teams state their current hypothesis for which production path they support. Their answers may also shed light on how well they've understood the information thus far.
Timer paused — 0 sec remaining.
Chapter 2 ended — showing feedback.
Chapter 3: The Recommendation has started.

What is this chapter about?
Teams make their pitch to Zena, saying which production path they recommend using and why. Carlos will also be in the meeting, and teams can call on him to answer specific questions. Zena will push not just for the recommendation, but for the underlying reasoning.

What to look for:
  • What do teams recommend?
  • How well do they defend their recommendation?
  • Are the able to convince Zena and earn her trust?
Timer adjusted by +1 min — 15 min 30 sec remaining.
Remember to move around to listen to teams' discussions. Sometimes the most insightful comments are said from one participant to another, rather than to an AI character.

Suggestion: You might consider using the Send Message feature to remind participants:

As you talk with Zena, try to articulate the assumptions in your model and what you will watch for as the rollout begins.
Timer adjusted by +1 min — 3 min 36 sec remaining.

Debrief Reminder: Now it's time to bring it all together in the final debrief!
  • Show Snapshot in the Debrief tools to show what happened next. If any teams earned "Market Maker," ask them how they achieved that.
  • Show Approaches or use the examples in the slides to show how teams supported their recommendation with additional context and judgment.
  • Finally, use Reflections to ask any additional questions that seem helpful for your audience to carry this learning forward with them.

Chapter 3 ended — showing feedback.
Case completed — all chapters finished.
